papers.title: Diversity of complementary diet and early food allergy risk
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Diet diversity (DD) in infancy may be protective for early food allergy (FA) but there is limited knowledge about how DD incorporating consumption frequency influences FA risk. METHODS: Three measures of DD were investigated in 2060 infants at 6 and/or at 9 months of age within the NorthPop Birth Cohort Study: a weighted DD score based on intake frequency, the number of introduced foods, and the number of introduced allergenic foods. In multivariable logistic regression models based on directed acyclic graphs, associations to parentally reported physician-diagnosed FA at age 9 and 18 months were estimated, including sensitivity and stratified analyses. RESULTS: High weighted DD scores (24-31p) at age 9 months were associated with 61% decreased odds of FA at age 18 months [OR (95% CI) = 0.39 0.18-0.88] compared with infants with the lowest DD scores (0-17p). The association remained significant after exclusion of early FA cases. Having introduced 13-14 foods at age 9 months, independent of consumption frequency, was associated with 45% decreased odds of FA [OR (95% CI) = 0.55 (0.31-0.98)] compared to having introduced 0-10 foods. When stratifying, significantly reduced odds for FA were seen for children with eczema and for children with no FA history in the family. No association was seen between DD at age 6 months and FA at age 18 months. CONCLUSION: A diverse diet at age 9 months may prevent FA at age 18 months. Our results underscore the need for additional investigations on the impact of consumption frequency in infancy.

papers.title: Role of skin management in the prevention of atopic dermatitis and food allergy
papers.abstract: Food allergy is postulated to originate from cutaneous sensitization through a disrupted skin barrier, particularly in atopic dermatitis (AD). Strategies for food allergy prevention currently centre around early allergic food introduction, but there is now increasing evidence for the role of early skin barrier restoration in the form of prophylactic emollient therapy and early aggressive, proactive treatment of established AD for food allergy prevention. Research gaps that remain to be addressed include the type of emollient or anti-inflammatory medication, which confers the greatest efficacy in preventive or proactive skin treatment, respectively, the duration of therapy, and the window of opportunity for these interventions.

papers.title: Translating research into practice: What’s new in the 2021 EAACI food allergy prevention guidelines?
papers.abstract: Given that food allergy (FA) is often lifelong and results in a significant reduction in quality of life for children and families, parents often ask “How can I stop my child developing FA?” This is especially true when there is a strong family history of FA or other atopic diseases. Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) are statements that include recommendations intended to optimize patient care and are informed by a systematic review of evidence containing an assessment of the benefit and harms. Following appropriate dissemination CPGs for FA prevention seek to inform practice by educating and updating healthcare professionals (HCP) and the wider community. Various explanations for FA development have been proposed, but the lack of “dual allergen exposure hypothesis” is the best-substantiated in recent research. The translation of this hypothesis into practice, by giving an infant allergenic food as soon as he/she is ready to be weaned, offers the most efficacious and practical evidence-based FA prevention strategy to date. In the past 5 years, several allergy societies and one national government (USA) have updated their allergy prevention guidance to incorporate “dual allergen hypothesis” evidence. Whilst the specifics of this advice vary, all encourage parents to introduce one or more allergenic foods in the first year of life. This is the result of a stepwise process, over the last 15 years. Such changes in Australian infant feeding guidelines resulted in a 16% reduction in peanut allergy in the first year of life.1 These remarkable data highlight that effective translation and dissemination of research findings into policy and guidance, results in substantial individual and population-level health benefits. These benefits will be associated with reduced morbidity and healthcare costs. The European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI), which brings together members from 124 countries and 50 National Allergy societies, recently updated the 2014 guideline on food allergy prevention in infants and young children.2 These updated guidelines help HCP provide evidence-based advice during critical time-points, from pregnancy, breastfeeding and alternate infant milk formula where breastfeeding is not possible, to weaning on to complementary foods. The update emphasizes the dearth of evidence regarding dietary modifications such as avoidance or consumption of common allergens and fish oil during pregnancy or breastfeeding. The updated guideline differs from the 2014 recommendations, which suggested a beneficial effect of fish oil intake in reducing FA onset; no such recommendation is now made. Interestingly, the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy does recommend consumption of fish oil during pregnancy and breastfeeding to prevent early life eczema. Intervention trials are currently investigating this strategy to prevent peanut and hen's egg allergy. Breastfeeding has a myriad of health benefits for both mother and child and should always be encouraged. However, appropriate alternatives are needed for infants of mothers who are unable or unwilling to breastfeed exclusively. Ethical challenges in performing breastfeeding trials have resulted in a lack of robust evidence regarding the role of breastfeeding and formula supplementation in FA prevention. A new recommendation from the EAACI update is to avoid supplementing breastfeeding (BF) with cow's milk formula in the first week of life. This recommendation is mainly based on a single RCT, which randomized breastfed infants who were at high risk of FA (atopic first-degree relative) to daily supplementation with cow's milk formula (CMF) (BF/CMF group) or supplementation of breastfeeding with elemental formula (EF) if needed (BF/EF) not limited to the first week of life.3 At 5 and 24 months, infants in the BF/CMF group had a higher risk of CM sensitization than those randomized to BF/CMF. More infants in the BF/CMF group also developed CMA, although the study was not powered to assess the effect of this difference. The Urashima study has several methodological limitations which restrict the utility of the findings. These are discussed in greater detail in the original paper and accompanying editorial.4 However, the notable finding from the Urashima study, that temporary supplementation with CMF may increase the risk of CMA, has also been noted in two cohort studies.5, 6 The mechanisms which underlie these findings are unclear. Given the limitations of available evidence, EAACI have deemed the advice to avoid CMF in the first week of life to be a low certainty recommendation and proposes that, if needed, HCP consider alternatives, alongside the family's specific circumstances. HCP should be open that this finding relates only to temporary supplementation–there is no clear evidence that prolonged supplementation with CMF whilst breastfeeding increases the risk of CMA–and the low certainty nature of recommendation. The update does not advise using any hydrolysed formula (partial, extensive, whey or casein) for allergy prevention; this is a change from the 2014 guideline, which recommended a documented hypoallergenic formula if breastmilk supplementation was required in the first four months of life. The updated guideline highlights that, as there is no evidence these formulae increase the risk of food allergy, they may serve as alternatives where breastfeeding is not possible. The update continues to advocate against the use of soy-based formulae for allergy prevention. In summary, there are no strongly recommended interventions for CMA prevention. The update proactively supports the introduction of peanut and hen's egg between 4–6 months of age for FA prevention. There is no recommendation for other common allergens, and whilst the EAT Study investigated the effect of the introduction of milk, wheat, fish and sesame at 4–6 months, there was no effect in the intention-to-treat analysis.7 The update makes no recommendation as to the quantity of food to be consumed, but a recent publication comparing prevention cohorts showed that 2 g of protein per week seems sufficient. This quantity should facilitate adherence to oral tolerance induction programs, especially if multiple food allergens are introduced. Importantly, infants who consume <2 g per week are at no greater risk of FA than those who consume these foods after 6 months of age. Whilst the previous EAACI guideline on allergy prevention (2014) drew only on the findings of the cross-sectional UK/Israel study, this update2 includes the Learning Early About Peanuts (LEAP) study and EAT study findings (As with the NIAID and the Australian guidelines, the update recommends peanut introduction to all infants, regardless of risk level, as a substantial number of children who do not meet “high risk” criteria will benefit from peanut oral tolerance induction (OTI). Importantly, peanut OTI is a feasible and safe intervention for growth and nutrition, but the immune benefits are allergen-specific.8 The update restricts the advice for early peanut introduction to countries with a high prevalence of peanut allergy, reflecting the populations’ conditions where the intervention trials were conducted. The update drew upon several OTI trials published since the original guideline was developed in 2014. Introducing egg, in a well-cooked form by 6 months of age, during the beginning of complementary feeding, is safe and offers protection against egg allergy.2 The update did not include a recently published analysis of the high-risk EAT population which found a reduced risk of egg allergy in the early introduction group (EIG).9 This provides further evidence that introducing well-cooked egg once weaning commences prevents egg allergy. In infancy, the introduction of other forms of egg such as pasteurized or raw has caused severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and thus is not recommended. Despite considering many allergy prevention strategies (Table 1), the EAACI guidelines found only one effective strategy; introducing peanut and egg as soon as weaning commences prevents peanut and egg allergy. HCP should recommend infants are given peanut from 4–6 months of age (in countries with high rates of peanut allergy) alongside continued breastfeeding and may recommend introducing well-cooked egg at the same time-point. The updated guideline suggests that if mothers need or choose to supplement EBF with formula, HCPs should discuss the low certainty possible risks of increased milk allergy through temporary supplementation with CMF during the first week of life. When discussing FA prevention strategies, HCPs should not recommend using hydrolysed or amino acid formulas over breastfeeding. Breastfeeding should always be promoted for its many other benefits. (i) Peanut protein (in an age-appropriate form such as peanut butter) may be given once developmentally ready and in line with family preferences (ii) Where children have an increased risk of peanut allergy (e.g. severe eczema or egg allergy) giving peanut protein proactively once weaning commences may reduce risk of new onset peanut allergy MAMM and HF declare that they have no relevant conflict of interest.
